listeningParts.title: Opening a student bank account
listeningParts.contextDescription: A new international student phones a bank to arrange a student account.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Northgate Bank, you're speaking to Fiona. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi. I've just arrived to start a degree at the university here, and I'd like to open a bank account. Someone told me you have special accounts for students.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: We do, yes. It's called the Student Plus account, and it's designed for people in full-time higher education. I can take some details now and then book you an appointment at a branch to finish things off. Is that all right?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Sure, that's great.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Lovely. First of all, what are you studying, and for how long?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'm doing a three-year degree in Accounting. I was going to do Economics, actually, but I changed my mind at the last minute.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Accounting. Well, you'll be good at keeping track of your money, then! Could I have your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Daniel Okafor. That's O-K-A-F-O-R.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Thank you, Daniel. And your date of birth?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: The twenty-third of June, 2006.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: And where are you living at the moment?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'm in a student flat. It's Flat 3, 27 Wharf Street. That's W-H-A-R-F. It's near the river, just behind the old customs house.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: I know it. Now, when you come in to the branch, you'll need to bring two things. The first is your passport, so we can check your identity. The second is something to prove you're a student and that you live at that address. Most people bring a letter from the university, which the student services office can print for you. A bill is no good, I'm afraid, because most students don't have bills in their own name.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay, a letter from student services. I'll get that tomorrow. Can I ask what the account actually offers? Is there a monthly charge?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: There's no monthly fee at all. You get a contactless debit card, online and mobile banking, and an arranged overdraft with no interest.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: How much is the overdraft?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: In your first year, you can borrow up to five hundred pounds interest-free. That goes up to a thousand pounds in your second and third years, if you've managed the account well. But I'd always say, only use it if you really need to, because it does have to be paid back once you graduate.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Right. I'll try not to touch it. What about the card? How long does it take to arrive?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Once the account's open, the card is posted to you and should arrive within five working days. Your PIN comes separately, a couple of days later, for security reasons.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: And is there a charge if I use the card abroad? I'll be going home to Canada at Christmas.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: With the Student Plus account, there's no fee for spending abroad, but if you take out cash from a machine overseas, there's a small charge. The other thing I'd recommend is our mobile app. If you lose your card, you can freeze it instantly from your phone, and unfreeze it if you find it again, rather than having to cancel it completely.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's handy. I'm always losing things.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: You're not the only one! Now, let's book that appointment. Our nearest branch to you is on Market Square. I'm afraid Tuesday is fully booked because it's the start of term, but I've got a slot on Thursday at half past two. Would that suit you?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Thursday's fine. I don't have any lectures in the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Just so you know, the branch is right next to the bus station, so it's easy to find. If you can't make it for any reason, please ring us at least a day in advance, so we can offer the slot to someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Perfect. The appointment should take about forty minutes. And how would you prefer us to contact you, by email or text?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Text, please. I don't check my email very often, to be honest.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: No problem. I'll send you a reminder by text the day before. Finally, just for our records, how did you hear about us?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: A friend from my course recommended you. She opened an account here last week.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Wonderful. Well, Daniel, that's everything for now. We'll see you on Thursday, and don't forget your passport and the letter.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I won't. Thanks very much for your help, Fiona.

listeningParts.title: Welcome to Castlegate Market
listeningParts.contextDescription: The manager of a historic covered market speaks to a group of new stallholders.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Castlegate Market. My name's Rosa Bellamy, and I've been the market manager here for about six years. I know some of you have run stalls at other markets before, while for others this is your very first business, so I'll try to cover the basics and you can ask questions at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Let me start with a little history, because people often ask about it. There's been a market on this site since the thirteenth century, when the town was granted a royal charter allowing it to hold a weekly market. For most of that time it was an open-air market, selling mainly livestock and grain. The covered hall we're standing in now was built much later, in 1878, and the iron and glass roof was restored about ten years ago, with help from a heritage grant. If you look up, you can still see the original ironwork, which was made in a foundry just outside the town.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, a lot of people assume that markets like ours are dying because of supermarkets and online shopping. In fact, our footfall, that's the number of visitors, has gone up every year since the restoration. What's changed is who comes and why. We get fewer people doing their whole weekly shop here, but far more people coming for things they can't get elsewhere: local cheeses, handmade goods, street food. So my advice is to focus on what makes your stall different, rather than trying to compete on price with the big shops.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Some practical points. The market's open Tuesday to Saturday, from eight until five thirty. Your rent is paid monthly, in advance, and it covers your pitch, cleaning of the common areas and security. You'll be glad to hear that we don't charge extra for heating in winter. What we do insist on is that you're open on at least four of the five market days, because empty stalls make the whole market look less lively and that affects everyone's trade.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Payment's another thing I get asked about. Almost all our traders now accept cards, and I'd strongly encourage you to do the same. We've found that customers who pay by card tend to spend more per visit than those using cash, partly because they're not limited by what's in their wallet. That said, quite a few of our older customers still prefer cash, so please don't go card-only.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Right, let me tell you about the facilities, because there have been some changes recently. Deliveries come in through the loading bay at the back, on Mill Lane. You can use it free of charge, but only before nine in the morning, because after that the lane gets very busy with pedestrians.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: For those of you selling food, there's a cold store next to the office, with refrigerated space for meat, fish and dairy. Space there is limited, so you need to book it in advance through the office, and there's a small weekly fee.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The recycling area used to be inside the hall, near the east entrance, but it's recently moved outside to the yard, because of complaints about the smell in summer. Please sort cardboard, glass and food waste into the right bins.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: If you need somewhere to keep your stock overnight, there are storage lockers in the basement. You'll need to collect a key from the office, and we ask for a deposit, which you get back when you return it.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: And finally, the electricity points. Every pitch has one, but the ones on the north side of the hall are being replaced at the moment, so they're closed for repairs until the end of the month. If you're on that side and you need power, have a word with me and we'll sort out a temporary cable.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Okay, that's the main things. Oh, one last point: we run a monthly late-night market on the first Friday of every month, with music and extra food stalls. It's optional, but it's very popular and it's a great way to attract new customers. There's no extra rent for it, but you do need to let the office know by the Monday before if you'd like to take part. Now, who's got a question?

listeningParts.title: Preparing a seminar on comparative advantage
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two economics students, Priya and Jack, discuss a seminar presentation with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Okay, Priya, Jack, come and sit down. You're presenting next week on comparative advantage, aren't you? How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We've done most of the reading, and we've got a rough structure. We thought we'd start with the history, then explain the theory with a simple example, and finish with some criticisms.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That sounds sensible. Who are you starting with?

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: David Ricardo. His book, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, came out in 1817, and that's where the idea is usually said to come from. Although we did find that some historians think other writers had similar ideas a bit earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's true, and it's worth a sentence, but don't spend long on it. The audience will want to understand the idea itself. How are you going to explain it?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We were going to use Ricardo's own example: England and Portugal, producing cloth and wine. The surprising part is that, in his example, Portugal is better at producing both goods. It needs fewer workers for cloth and for wine. And yet both countries still gain from trade.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: Because what matters isn't absolute advantage, but opportunity cost. For Portugal, making cloth means giving up a lot of wine, so it's better to specialise in wine and buy cloth from England.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. But I've found students often get lost with Ricardo's original numbers. Have you thought about a more modern example?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We had one idea: a top lawyer who's also the fastest typist in her office. Should she do her own typing?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a classic, and it works well, because everyone can see that her time is more valuable spent on legal work, even though she types faster than her assistant. I'd open with that, actually, before Ricardo, to get people's attention, and then show that the same logic applies to countries.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: Okay, so swap the order. That makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Should we include any real figures about trade, like how much of the world's output is exported?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: One or two figures would be fine, as long as they're from a reliable source, such as the World Trade Organization or the World Bank, and you give the year. But don't overload the audience. The aim is to explain the idea clearly, not to impress people with statistics.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Now, the criticisms. What have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: The main one is that the theory assumes workers can move easily from one industry to another. In reality, if a factory closes because of cheap imports, the workers can't just become software engineers overnight. We found research on the effect of Chinese imports on manufacturing areas in the United States, which showed that job losses were concentrated in particular towns, and those places took many years to recover.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's the work by David Autor and his colleagues on what they called the China shock. It's very influential. Make sure you cite it properly. What else?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We also wanted to mention that the model is static. It looks at what countries are good at now, but countries can develop new advantages over time. South Korea, for example, wasn't an obvious place to build ships or electronics in the 1950s.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, and some economists argue that governments helped to create those advantages, by protecting young industries for a while. That's a debate you could leave open for the discussion questions. I'd be careful not to suggest that the theory is simply wrong, though. Most economists still accept the basic logic. The arguments are about who gains, who loses, and what should be done for the losers.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.text: So maybe we should end with policy, like retraining programmes?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. That gives the presentation a clear conclusion. How long is it at the moment?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: About twenty-five minutes, but we're only allowed twenty.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then cut the history section down. And one more thing: last year, several groups put far too much text on their slides. Use a diagram for the England and Portugal example instead. It's much clearer.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We'll do that. Could we send you the slides before Friday?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Send them by Thursday evening, and I'll give you comments on Friday morning.

listeningParts.title: The evolution of money
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an introductory economics course on how money developed over time.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to step back from the models we've been looking at and ask a very basic question: what is money, and where did it come from? Economists usually say that money has three functions. It's a medium of exchange, which means we use it to buy things. It's a unit of account, so we can compare the value of very different goods. And it's a store of value, meaning that we can save it and spend it later.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The traditional story, which you'll find in many textbooks, is that before money, people used barter, swapping goods directly. The problem with barter is what the nineteenth-century economist William Stanley Jevons called the double coincidence of wants. If I have fish and want shoes, I have to find someone who has shoes and who, at the same moment, wants fish. Money, the story goes, was invented to solve this problem.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: I should say that many anthropologists are sceptical about this story. They point out that there's very little evidence of whole societies that ran on barter. In small communities, people more often relied on systems of credit and obligation: I give you something now, and you owe me a favour later. So it may be that keeping records of debts came before coins, not after them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Whatever its origins, early money often took the form of commodities that had value in themselves, or were at least scarce and durable. Grain, cattle and salt were all used in different places. One of the most widespread was the cowrie shell, which was used as money across large parts of Africa and Asia for centuries. Shells were ideal in some ways: they're durable, difficult to fake, and easy to count. In some regions, they remained in use until the early twentieth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first coins appeared in the seventh century BC, in Lydia, in what's now western Turkey. They were made from electrum, a natural mixture of gold and silver, and stamped with a design to show that their weight and purity were guaranteed. That stamp was important. It meant that people no longer had to weigh metal every time they made a purchase; they could simply count the coins.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The next major step happened in China. Carrying large quantities of metal coins was heavy and inconvenient, and during the Song dynasty, around the eleventh century, the government began issuing paper money. Marco Polo, who visited China in the thirteenth century, was astonished that people would accept pieces of paper in exchange for goods. In Europe, banknotes came much later. The first in Europe were issued in Sweden, in 1661, by a bank called Stockholms Banco, although the bank soon got into trouble for printing too many of them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For much of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, many countries operated a gold standard. Under this system, a banknote could, in principle, be exchanged at the bank for a fixed amount of gold. This limited how much money governments could create, which helped to keep prices stable, but it also made it hard to respond to economic crises.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: After the Second World War, the Bretton Woods agreement of 1944 created a system in which other currencies were fixed to the US dollar, and the dollar itself was linked to gold. That arrangement ended in 1971, when President Nixon announced that the United States would no longer exchange dollars for gold. Since then, the major currencies have been what economists call fiat money: money that has value not because it can be exchanged for anything, but because governments declare it to be legal tender, and because people trust that others will accept it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: And that brings us to the central point of today's lecture. Money, ultimately, is a system of trust. A banknote is just paper, and the numbers in your bank account are just entries in a computer. They work only because we're confident that they'll be accepted tomorrow. When that confidence collapses, as it does in a hyperinflation, money can lose almost all its value very quickly. Next week, we'll look at the role of central banks in maintaining that trust.

readingPassages.title: The roads of silk
paragraphs: The phrase 'Silk Road' suggests a single highway along which camels carried bales of silk from China to Rome. The reality was far more complicated. The term itself is relatively modern: it was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen, who was mapping possible railway routes across Asia. What he described was not one road but a shifting network of overland routes, linking China with Central Asia, India, Persia and the Mediterranean, that carried goods, people and ideas for well over a thousand years.

The origins of the network are usually traced to the second century BC, when the Han dynasty in China sent an official named Zhang Qian westwards on a diplomatic mission. His aim was to find allies against the Xiongnu, a nomadic people who threatened China's northern frontier. Zhang Qian was captured and held for around ten years before he escaped and continued his journey, finally returning to the Chinese capital some thirteen years after he had set out. He failed to secure an alliance, but the reports he brought back of wealthy kingdoms to the west, and of their powerful horses, encouraged the Han emperors to extend their control along the trade routes.

Silk was certainly one of the most valuable goods traded. Its production was a closely guarded Chinese secret, and in the Roman world it became a symbol of luxury. Roman writers complained about the fashion for silk clothing, which they considered immoral, and the scholar Pliny the Elder grumbled that enormous sums of money were flowing out of the empire to pay for luxury goods from the East. However, silk was only one item among many. Spices, precious stones, glass, paper, horses and metalwork all moved along the routes, in both directions. Chinese buyers, for instance, valued glassware from the Roman world and the Middle East, which was rare and expensive in China.

Surprisingly few merchants ever travelled the entire distance. Instead, goods passed from hand to hand, changing owners many times, with each trader covering only one section of the journey. Some peoples became specialists in this middleman role. The Sogdians, from the region around Samarkand in present-day Uzbekistan, established trading communities across Central Asia and China, and their language became widely used in commerce. At each stage, prices rose, so that by the time silk reached the Mediterranean it was many times more expensive than in China.

Travel was slow and dangerous. Caravans crossed deserts, such as the Taklamakan, and some of the highest mountain ranges on Earth. The two-humped Bactrian camel was ideal for these conditions, since it can carry heavy loads and survive both freezing winters and scorching summers. Along the main routes, caravanserais, or roadside inns, offered travellers and their animals shelter for the night. Oasis towns grew rich by providing water, food and markets, and some, such as Kashgar and Dunhuang, became important centres of culture as well as trade.

Ideas travelled along the routes as readily as goods. Buddhism spread from India into Central Asia and China, and the cave temples at Dunhuang contain thousands of Buddhist paintings and manuscripts. Technologies also moved. Knowledge of how to make paper, invented in China, had reached the Islamic world by the eighth century, and later spread to Europe. Silk production itself eventually escaped China's control: according to the Byzantine historian Procopius, monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople in the sixth century AD, allowing a silk industry to develop there.

Not everything that travelled was welcome. Historians believe that the Black Death, the plague that devastated Asia, the Middle East and Europe in the fourteenth century, spread partly along the trade routes that connected these regions. Merchants, soldiers and their animals carried not only goods but also the fleas and rats that transmitted the disease. In this sense, the Silk Roads were an early example of a familiar feature of globalisation: the same connections that spread wealth and knowledge could also spread disaster.

From the fifteenth century onwards, the overland routes gradually declined in importance as European sailors opened sea routes around Africa to India and East Asia, which could carry larger quantities of goods more cheaply. Yet the memory of the Silk Roads has never disappeared. In 2014, a 5,000-kilometre section of the network between China and Central Asia was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List, nominated jointly by China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Today, the name is often used for new infrastructure projects, a sign of how powerfully the idea of these ancient connections still shapes the way we think about trade.

readingPassages.title: When money melts away
paragraphs: Most people are used to prices rising slowly. In many countries, central banks aim for inflation of around two per cent a year, a rate at which most people barely notice that their money is losing value. Occasionally, however, inflation spirals out of control. In 1956, the American economist Phillip Cagan proposed a definition that is still widely used: hyperinflation begins when prices rise by more than fifty per cent in a single month. At that rate, prices increase roughly a hundredfold within a year, and money rapidly loses its usefulness.

The most famous case occurred in Germany in the early 1920s. After the First World War, the German government faced enormous debts, including reparation payments to the victorious Allies. When Germany fell behind with these payments, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, the country's industrial heartland, in January 1923. The government encouraged workers there to go on strike and continued to pay their wages, financing this by printing ever larger quantities of money. By November 1923, one US dollar was worth around 4.2 trillion marks.

Even this was not the worst hyperinflation in history. That record belongs to Hungary, whose economy had been devastated by the Second World War. In July 1946, prices in Hungary were doubling roughly every fifteen hours. Banknotes were printed with ever greater numbers of zeros, until the old currency, the pengő, became practically worthless and was replaced by the forint. More recently, Zimbabwe experienced hyperinflation in the late 2000s, following a collapse in agricultural output and heavy money printing. In 2009, the country's central bank issued a note worth one hundred trillion Zimbabwean dollars, shortly before the currency was abandoned altogether.

Although each case has its own history, the underlying mechanism is usually similar. A government that cannot raise enough money through taxes or borrowing begins to pay its bills by creating new money. As more money chases the same quantity of goods, prices rise. The crucial moment comes when people start to expect further rises. They then try to spend their money as quickly as possible, before it loses more value, and this rush to spend pushes prices up even faster. Inflation, in other words, can feed on itself. At its most extreme stage, people may refuse to accept the national currency at all, and the government finds that even printing money no longer pays its bills, since the notes lose value before they can be spent.

Daily life under hyperinflation becomes exhausting. In Germany in 1923, workers were sometimes paid twice a day so that they could rush out and spend their wages before prices rose again. Restaurants were reported to change their prices while customers were still eating. Many people abandoned money altogether and returned to barter, exchanging goods and services directly, while others used foreign currencies wherever possible. Businesses found it almost impossible to plan, since they could not know what their costs would be from one week to the next. Photographs from the period show children playing with bundles of worthless notes.

Hyperinflation does not harm everyone equally. Those who suffer most are people who depend on savings or fixed incomes, such as pensioners, whose money can become worthless within months. In Germany, many middle-class families who had saved carefully for decades lost almost everything. On the other hand, people who owed money often benefited, because their debts shrank in real terms. Some property owners in Germany were able to pay off their mortgages with money that was worth only a tiny fraction of what they had originally borrowed.

Ending a hyperinflation usually requires more than one measure. In Germany, a new currency, the Rentenmark, was introduced in November 1923, with one Rentenmark replacing one trillion old marks. Just as important, the government strictly limited the number of new notes and took steps to bring its spending under control. The key, economists argue, is credibility: people must believe that the government will not simply print money again. Without that belief, a new currency is likely to suffer the same fate as the old one.

The memory of hyperinflation can last for generations. In Germany, the experience of 1923 is often said to explain why the post-war central bank, the Bundesbank, placed such great emphasis on keeping prices stable, an approach that later influenced the design of the European Central Bank. For economists, the lesson of these episodes is that money depends on trust. When people stop believing that the money in their pockets will hold its value, even a modern economy can find that its currency melts away with astonishing speed.

readingPassages.title: Should we say goodbye to cash?
paragraphs: For most of history, money meant something you could hold in your hand. Today, in many countries, notes and coins are becoming a rarity. People tap cards and phones to pay for coffee, transfer money to friends with an app, and may go weeks without touching a banknote. Some governments, banks and economists welcome this trend and would like to speed it up. Others worry that a cashless society would leave some people behind and give too much power to those who run payment systems. The question of whether cash has a future is no longer a theoretical one.

Sweden is often described as the country closest to abandoning cash. Surveys by its central bank, the Riksbank, have found that fewer than one in ten Swedes used cash for their most recent purchase in a shop, and many cafés and even some bank branches no longer accept it. Yet the speed of this change has caused concern. Swedish lawmakers have required the largest banks to continue providing cash services, and the Riksbank has investigated issuing a digital currency of its own, partly so that the public would still have access to money issued directly by the state.

In some developing economies, digital payments have spread for different reasons. In Kenya, the mobile money service M-Pesa, launched by the telecommunications company Safaricom in 2007, allows people to send and receive money by text message, even on basic mobile phones and without a bank account. A study by the economists Tavneet Suri and William Jack, published in 2016, estimated that access to M-Pesa had lifted around two per cent of Kenyan households out of extreme poverty, in part because it made it easier for families to receive help from relatives during hard times.

Supporters of a cashless economy make several arguments. Digital payments are fast and convenient, and they leave a record, which makes tax evasion and crimes such as money laundering harder. The Harvard economist Kenneth Rogoff, in his 2016 book The Curse of Cash, argued that large-denomination banknotes are used disproportionately in illegal activity and should be phased out, while smaller notes could remain. Rogoff also pointed out that the existence of cash limits the ability of central banks to set negative interest rates, because people can simply withdraw their savings and keep them as notes.

However, attempts to force a rapid move away from cash can cause serious problems. In November 2016, the Indian government suddenly withdrew its 500- and 1,000-rupee notes, which together made up around eighty-six per cent of the cash in circulation by value. The aim was to tackle corruption and counterfeit money. The result was weeks of long queues at banks and severe difficulties for small traders and farmers who relied on cash. A later report by the Reserve Bank of India found that almost all of the withdrawn money had been returned to banks, suggesting that relatively little illegal wealth had been eliminated.

There are also concerns about who benefits from a cashless world. In China, two private platforms, Alipay and WeChat Pay, handle a very large share of everyday transactions, which are usually made by scanning QR codes with a smartphone. This is extremely convenient, but it means that a small number of companies hold detailed information about what hundreds of millions of people buy. In my view, this concentration of data is one of the strongest arguments for keeping cash. A banknote does not record where it was spent, and it does not depend on a company's willingness to process a payment.

The groups most dependent on cash are often those with the least power to complain: elderly people, those on low incomes, people with disabilities and those living in remote areas with poor internet connections. For them, a sudden disappearance of cash would not be a minor inconvenience. Digital systems also fail. Power cuts, technical faults and cyber-attacks can all prevent electronic payments, sometimes for hours or days. In my view, any society that relies entirely on digital payments is taking an unnecessary risk, since cash continues to work when the network does not.

None of this means that the trend towards digital money should be reversed, nor would that be possible. The convenience is real, and services like M-Pesa have brought clear benefits. But I believe the choice should remain with the public. Governments should ensure that cash remains widely available and accepted for as long as people want to use it, and should treat it as a piece of public infrastructure, like roads or libraries, rather than as an outdated technology waiting to be retired. A cashless society may arrive one day, but it should arrive because people choose it, not because they are given no alternative.
